source_refs.note: Exercise 10.2 Q2 (i)-(ii), book p.189 (PDF 194); proofs (no answer-key entry). Checked with sympy; solution book PDF 898-900 agrees.

blocks.explanation:
A proof: start from the left side and reach the right side.
The left side is the sine of a sum, so expand it.
Plan: \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\) formula, put \(\sin 45^{\circ} = \cos 45^{\circ} = 1/\sqrt{2}\), take the common factor.
steps:
Given: the identity to prove.
To prove: L.H.S. \(= \sin(45^{\circ} + \alpha)\) equals R.H.S. \(= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\sin\alpha + \cos\alpha)\).
Method: Expand the L.H.S. with
\[\sin(A + B) = \sin A\cos B + \cos A\sin B\]

Put in the special values
\[= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\alpha + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\alpha\]
Why: \(\sin 45^{\circ} = \cos 45^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Take out the common factor
\[= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\sin\alpha + \cos\alpha) = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: Both terms have \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\); order inside the bracket does not matter.

Check with \(\alpha = 45^{\circ}\)
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \sin 90^{\circ} = 1\]
\[\text{R.H.S.} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 1 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A quick numerical test confirms the identity.

blocks.explanation:
A proof with the cosine of a sum.
Expand the left side and use the values at \(45^{\circ}\).
Plan: \(\cos(A + B)\) formula, then take out \(1/\sqrt{2}\).
steps:
Given: the identity to prove.
To prove: \(\cos(\alpha + 45^{\circ}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\cos\alpha - \sin\alpha)\).
Method: Expand the L.H.S. with
\[\cos(A + B) = \cos A\cos B - \sin A\sin B\]

Expand the left side
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \cos(\alpha + 45^{\circ})\]
\[= \cos\alpha\cos 45^{\circ} - \sin\alpha\sin 45^{\circ}\]
Why: \(A = \alpha\), \(B = 45^{\circ}\); for cosine a plus in the angle gives a minus.

Put in the special values
\[= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\alpha - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\alpha\]
Why: \(\cos 45^{\circ} = \sin 45^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Take out the common factor
\[= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\cos\alpha - \sin\alpha) = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) is common to both terms.

Check with \(\alpha = 45^{\circ}\)
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \cos 90^{\circ} = 0\]
\[\text{R.H.S.} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(0) = 0 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Both sides agree.
